qhtml:
Choose the correct indirect narration of the following statement from the given alternatives:
Salini said to Meena, "Why did you not tell the truth to my friend when he was in real trouble?"
opts: Salini asked Meena why she had not told the truth to her friend when he had been in real trouble.
Salini asked Meena why he had not told the truth to her friend when she was in real trouble.
Salini asked Meena that why she had not told the truth to her friend when she had been in real trouble.
Salini asked Meena why she had not told the truth to his friend when he had in real trouble.
expl:
Rule: wh-question → indirect speech (प्रश्नवाचक वाक्य का अप्रत्यक्ष कथन):

• said to → asked

• keep the wh-word (why) as the joiner — no that; put the sentence in statement order, no question mark

• past reporting verb: did … not tell (simple past) → had not told (past perfect); was → had been

• pronouns: you (Meena) → she; my (Salini's) → her; he (the friend) stays he

Example: He said to me, "Why did you leave?" → He asked me why I had left.

Apply it.

Why did you not tell → why she had not told

my friend → her friend

he was → he had been

Answer: (1) Salini asked Meena why she had not told the truth to her friend when he had been in real trouble.

Why the others are wrong.

• why he had not told … when she was — the pronouns are swapped: Meena is she, the friend is he (सर्वनाम की भूल).

• asked Meena that why — that is never added before a wh-word in an indirect question (that + why साथ नहीं); the friend also wrongly becomes she.

• his friend … when he had in real trouble — my (Salini's) must become her, and had in lacks the verb been (क्रिया छूटी).

Indirect wh-questions: the wh-word is the joiner — never "that why".

•why he had not told … when she was — the pronouns are swapped: Meena is she, the friend is he (सर्वनाम की भूल).

•asked Meena that why — that is never added before a wh-word in an indirect question (that + why साथ नहीं); the friend also wrongly becomes she.

•his friend … when he had in real trouble — my (Salini's) must become her, and had in lacks the verb been (क्रिया छूटी).

Indirect wh-questions: the wh-word is the joiner — never "that why".

qhtml: What is the antonym of "Obdurate"?
expl:
Meaning: obdurate = stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or action (हठी, अड़ियल).

Its opposite is compliant = ready to obey or agree (आज्ञाकारी, सहज मानने वाला).

Answer: (3) Compliant

Why the others are wrong.

• adamant = refusing to be persuaded (अटल, दृढ़) — a synonym of obdurate.

• inflexible = unwilling to change (अनम्य) — also a synonym.

• unyielding = not giving way (न झुकने वाला) — a third synonym.

Three of the four options mean "stubborn" — the odd one out is the antonym.

qhtml:
Choose the option that is the most appropriate conversion of the following sentence into Direct Speech.
Shalini asked Yusuf if he would go to her party that night.
opts: Shalini asked Yusuf, “Would you go to my party this night?”
Shalini said to Yusuf, “Will you come to my party that night?”
Shalini said to Yusuf, “Will you come to my party tonight?”
Shalini asked Yusuf, “You will come to my party tonight?”
expl:
Rule: indirect yes/no question → direct speech (अप्रत्यक्ष से प्रत्यक्ष कथन):

• asked → said to

• drop if/whether; use question order (auxiliary before subject) and end with ?

• would → will; that night → tonight

• he (Yusuf, the listener) → you; her (Shalini's) → my

• go to a party one is invited to by the speaker → come (movement towards the speaker)

Example: She asked me if I would visit her that day. → She said to me, "Will you visit me today?"

Apply it.

if he would go → Will you come

her party → my party

that night → tonight

Answer: (3) Shalini said to Yusuf, “Will you come to my party tonight?”

Why the others are wrong.

• Would you go … this night — would is not changed back to will, and that night becomes tonight, not this night (this night अप्रचलित).

• that night — inside quotes the time word must return to the speaker's present: tonight (काल-सूचक शब्द नहीं बदला).

• You will come …? — statement order with a question mark; a direct question needs Will you (प्रश्न क्रम नहीं).

Back to direct: would → will, that night → tonight, her → my.

qhtml:
In the given passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage intently and choose the most appropriate option to fill in each blank:
Democracies are usually credited with being resilient, yet the past indicates that they can be quite vulnerable. Those institutions that are meant to protect freedom can weaken when citizens become disconnected or when politicians take advantage of (1) ______ within the system. Gradual removal of checks and balances might not raise an alarm until it is too late.
One of the central factors is the state of public discourse. When argument gets polarised and facts are sacrificed to (2) ______, democratic conventions start to disintegrate. The media is responsible here, either as a watchdog or as a megaphone for disinformation. The advent of echo chambers has made it simpler for individuals to shun (3) ______ perspectives, strengthening tribalism.
Economic inequality is another threat. When significant portions of the populace feel left out of prosperity, they can lose confidence in democratic processes and seek (4) ______ alternatives. This cynicism can be taken advantage of by populist movements that make quick fixes but destroy democratic ideas.
Democracy must be safeguarded with vigilance, participation, and a willingness to search for truth. Without these, even the most entrenched systems can become (5) ______, susceptible to rot from within.
What should come in the place of blank number 4?
expl:
The deciding words.

"they can lose confidence in democratic processes and seek (4) [blank] alternatives … populist movements that … destroy democratic ideas."

What the blank needs.

An alternative to democracy — a non-democratic form of rule.

authoritarian = demanding strict obedience to one ruler or group, without free choice (सत्तावादी, तानाशाही).

It is the direct opposite of the democratic processes people have lost faith in.

Answer: (3) Authoritarian

Why the others are wrong.

• violent = using physical force (हिंसक) — the passage speaks of systems of rule, not of force.

• radical = favouring sweeping change (आमूल परिवर्तनवादी) — a radical change can still be democratic; it does not name the anti-democratic choice.

• extremist = holding extreme political or religious views (चरमपंथी) — describes people's views, while the passage is contrasting forms of government.

Word help.

populace = the general public (जनसाधारण).

cynicism = distrust of people's motives and of institutions (निराशावाद, अविश्वास).

populist = claiming to speak for ordinary people against elites (लोकलुभावन).

Lose faith in democracy → turn to its opposite: authoritarian rule.

qhtml:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions based on the passage:
The story “The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse” is a pleasant and interesting one that highlights the purity of youthfulness and the strong moral values of the Armenian Garoghlanian tribe. The story revolves around the lives of two cousins, Aram and Mourad, who belong to a poor family but are known for their honest nature. Early one morning, Aram is amazed to see his cousin Mourad riding a beautiful white horse. As the boys could not afford such a horse, Aram suspects that the horse could have been ridden without permission, but his excitement to ride the horse makes him forget his suspicion momentarily.
The two boys spend a few days secretly enjoying the rides and feel a deep connection with the animal. However, when they meet the horse’s owner, John Byro, and hear his sad story, they feel a sense of guilt. Though Byro recognizes his horse, he is too impressed by the tribe’s reputation to accuse the boys. His faith in silence is deeply touching for the boys. Finally, Mourad decides to secretly return the horse to its proper stable.
The story beautifully depicts how good values and a high moral standard can direct young hearts in the right direction.
Why did the boys feel guilty after meeting John Byro?
opts: Because his sadness reminded them of their wrongdoing
Because he offered them money for returning the horse
expl:
The deciding line.

"when they meet the horse’s owner, John Byro, and hear his sad story, they feel a sense of guilt."

Read the cause.

The trigger is Byro's sad story — the loss of his horse.

Hearing the owner's sorrow makes them see that taking his horse was wrong.

So his sadness reminded them of their wrongdoing (उसके दुःख ने उन्हें अपनी ग़लती का एहसास कराया).

Answer: Because his sadness reminded them of their wrongdoing

Why the others are wrong.

• he scolded them harshly = told them off angrily (कड़ी डाँट लगाई) — he never scolds; his silence is what touches them.

• he accused them of theft = charged them with stealing (चोरी का आरोप लगाया) — the passage says the opposite: he is too impressed by the tribe's reputation to accuse the boys.

• he offered them money for returning the horse = a reward (इनाम की पेशकश) — no money is mentioned, and the horse is returned later, in secret.

Word help.

guilt = the feeling of having done wrong (अपराध-बोध).

Guilt came from sympathy, not from accusation — Byro said nothing against them.

qhtml:
Which of the following pairs of homonyms can be used to fill in the blanks most suitably?
During his ______ from the snowy peak, he thought about his ______ from a long line of mountaineers.
expl:
Meaning: descent has two meanings (दो अर्थ वाला शब्द):

• the act of coming down a slope (उतराई, अवरोहण)

• one's ancestry, lineage (वंश, कुल)

Apply it.

Blank 1 — coming down from the snowy peak → descent (going down).

Blank 2 — from a long line of mountaineers → descent (ancestry).

The same word fits both blanks — that is the homonym being tested.

Answer: (1) descent, descent

Why the others are wrong.

• descent, dissent — dissent = disagreement with an official view (असहमति); one cannot have "dissent from a long line of mountaineers" in the sense of family.

• dissent, descent — "his dissent from the snowy peak" makes no sense; one does not disagree with a mountain.

• dissent, dissent — neither blank is about disagreement.

De-SCENT goes down (a hill or a family tree); dis-SENT disagrees.

qhtml: Select the most appropriate synonym of the word: PROCLIVITY
expl:
Meaning: proclivity = a natural tendency or inclination to do something (प्रवृत्ति, झुकाव).

Example: He has a proclivity for exaggeration — he tends to exaggerate.

Its synonym is tendency = an inclination to act in a particular way (प्रवृत्ति, रुझान).

Answer: (3) Tendency

Why the others are wrong.

• aversion = strong dislike (अरुचि, घृणा) — the opposite of a leaning towards something.

• dislike = a feeling of not liking (नापसंद) — again the opposite direction.

• indifference = lack of interest or concern (उदासीनता) — no leaning either way, so not a tendency.

Pro-CLIV-ity: "leaning forward" (Latin clivus = slope) — you lean towards what you are prone to.

qhtml:
In the following question, out of the four alternatives, choose the one which gives the correct meaning of the given idiom or phrase.
Let's call it a day and start over tomorrow morning.
opts: To end the work for the day
expl:
Meaning: call it a day = to stop working for now, to decide one has done enough (आज का काम समाप्त करना).

"start over tomorrow morning" confirms that today's work is ending.

Origin.

From the 19th-century phrase call it half a day — a worker leaving early; it later became "call it a day", declaring the working day finished.

Answer: (3) To end the work for the day

Why the others are wrong.

• To start working for the day — the reverse; that is to get down to work or to start the day (काम शुरू करना).

• Give the day a specific name — a literal reading; the idiom has nothing to do with naming (नामकरण).

• Check the calendar for the date — another literal reading; that is just to look up the date (तारीख देखना).

Call it a day — and if it is evening, "call it a night".

qhtml:
Choose the best option to replace the underlined part to improve the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution.'
They decided to put up the launch indefinitely before their chairman was released from jail.
expl:
Meaning: put off = postpone, delay to a later time (स्थगित करना, टालना).

until = up to the time when (जब तक … नहीं).

Apply it.

A launch that waits for the chairman's release is postponed until he comes out.

They decided to put off the launch indefinitely until their chairman was released from jail.

Answer: (2) Put off the launch indefinitely until

Why the others are wrong.

• put up (the original) = to erect, or to give someone lodging (खड़ा करना / ठहराना); with before the sentence also loses its logic.

• put by = to save money for later (बचाकर रखना); and after reverses the time sense.

Put OFF = postpone; put ON = wear/stage; put UP = lodge/erect; put BY = save.

qhtml: Identify the incorrect sentence.
opts: Maria has bacame so fat after eating a lot of junk food in the hostel.
Every student has to take the preliminary test.
Korean web series is the best among all other series.
expl:
⚠️ Note: the official key marks option (a) and that is the intended answer, but option (d) is also faulty — a superlative cannot be followed by all other. The item has two incorrect sentences.

Rule: the present perfect is has / have + past participle (V3).

become has the forms become – became – become, so the V3 is become, not became.

Example: He has become a doctor. (not has became)

Find the error.

Sentence 1 has has bacame — a misspelt simple-past form after has.

Correct: Maria has become so fat after eating a lot of junk food in the hostel.

Answer: (1) Maria has bacame so fat after eating a lot of junk food in the hostel.

Why the others are fine.

• Every student has to take the preliminary test. — every takes a singular verb, so has is right; preliminary = initial, first-stage (प्रारंभिक).

• Beena is my sister's best friend. — the possessive sister's (one sister) and the superlative best are correct (सही वाक्य).

Given below are four jumbled sentences. Select the option that gives their correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
P: In addition, these ancient manuscripts provide profound insights into human consciousness.
Q: Therefore, modern scholars continue to analyze these texts for timeless wisdom.
R: Ancient Indian scriptures offer a vast treasure of philosophical and spiritual knowledge.
S: However, translating these complex Sanskrit verses remains a very difficult task.
expl:
Opener test.

R — Ancient Indian scriptures offer a vast treasure … — introduces the topic with no linking word and no pointer: the opener.

P (In addition, these), Q (Therefore, … these texts) and S (However, these) all lean on something said before.

Only option (a) begins with R.

Links.

R → P: In addition adds a second merit; these ancient manuscripts = R's ancient Indian scriptures.

P → S: However turns from the merits to the difficulty — translating these complex Sanskrit verses.

S → Q: Therefore draws the conclusion from the whole case — the texts are rich (R, P), so scholars continue to study them for timeless wisdom, difficulty (S) notwithstanding.

The paragraph.

Ancient Indian scriptures offer a vast treasure of philosophical and spiritual knowledge. In addition, these ancient manuscripts provide profound insights into human consciousness. However, translating these complex Sanskrit verses remains a very difficult task. Therefore, modern scholars continue to analyze these texts for timeless wisdom.

Answer: RPSQ

Word help.

profound = very deep (गहन, गहरा).

consciousness = awareness of the self and the world (चेतना).

In addition, However, Therefore — three connectors, none of which can start a paragraph.

The following sentence has two blanks. Choose the most suitable set of prepositions from the given options to fill in the blanks and complete the sentence meaningfully:
The athlete excelled ______ sprinting but faltered ______ long-distance events.
expl:
Rule: excel in / at a field or activity (किसी क्षेत्र में श्रेष्ठ होना); falter at a task or obstacle (पर लड़खड़ाना).

Example: She excels in mathematics but falters at public speaking.

Apply it.

excelled in sprinting — the field he was best in.

faltered at long-distance events — the point where he stumbled.

Answer: (1) in, at

Why the others are wrong.

• on, in — excel on is not used; on marks a surface or a day (सतह/दिन).

• in, by — by marks agent or means (के द्वारा); faltered by events turns the events into the cause, not the place of failure.

• with, at — excel with means "using" something (के साथ), not the field one is good in.

Excel IN a field, falter AT a hurdle.

In the given passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage intently and choose the most appropriate option to fill in each blank:
Democracies are usually credited with being resilient, yet the past indicates that they can be quite vulnerable. Those institutions that are meant to protect freedom can weaken when citizens become disconnected or when politicians take advantage of (1) ______ within the system. Gradual removal of checks and balances might not raise an alarm until it is too late.
One of the central factors is the state of public discourse. When argument gets polarised and facts are sacrificed to (2) ______, democratic conventions start to disintegrate. The media is responsible here, either as a watchdog or as a megaphone for disinformation. The advent of echo chambers has made it simpler for individuals to shun (3) ______ perspectives, strengthening tribalism.
Economic inequality is another threat. When significant portions of the populace feel left out of prosperity, they can lose confidence in democratic processes and seek (4) ______ alternatives. This cynicism can be taken advantage of by populist movements that make quick fixes but destroy democratic ideas.
Democracy must be safeguarded with vigilance, participation, and a willingness to search for truth. Without these, even the most entrenched systems can become (5) ______, susceptible to rot from within.
What should come in the place of blank number 3?
expl:
The deciding words.

"echo chambers … simpler for individuals to shun (3) [blank] perspectives, strengthening tribalism."

What the blank needs.

An echo chamber repeats your own view, so what you shun (टालना, दूर रहना) is the other side's view.

opposing = contrary, of the other side (विरोधी).

Shunning opposing views is exactly what strengthens tribalism.

Answer: (1) Opposing

Why the others are wrong.

• dissecting = cutting apart for close study (चीर-फाड़ कर विश्लेषण करने वाला) — a verb form that does not describe a perspective.

• critical = fault-finding or analytical (आलोचनात्मक) — weaker; tribalism is about rejecting the other camp, not just criticism.

• alternative = another available choice (वैकल्पिक) — neutral; it does not carry the us vs them sense that "tribalism" needs.

Word help.

echo chamber = a space where people hear only views that repeat their own (प्रतिध्वनि कक्ष — एक ही विचार की गूँज).

tribalism = strong loyalty to one's own group against others (गुटबाज़ी, कबीलाई निष्ठा).

Echo chamber = same voice in, opposing voice out.

qhtml:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions based on the passage:
The events in Rajamahendravaram in Andhra Pradesh involving the mass poisoning of consumers by milk contaminated with ethylene glycol sound a regulatory alarm. As of March 8, the death toll was 11, with approximately 20 other people, including infants, hospitalised. Milk is a staple in Indian households and contamination by an industrial compound already infamous in India for its lethality carries the potential to trigger a crisis of confidence in local, unbranded milk supplies. Children and the elderly are most affected by ethylene glycol poisoning due to their higher metabolic sensitivity and lower renal reserves, respectively. This could push people towards pasteurised milk from regulated cooperatives such as Amul or Vijaya, which seems desirable, but a large share of milk is also distributed in India through small vendors. Food-safety compliance is as much about punishing bad actors as about reducing the cost of doing the right thing. In the informal supply chain, cold-chain monitoring and hygiene inspections are almost entirely absent, leaving room for contamination. Subsidised testing kits and cooperative chilling facilities can thus reduce the risk at small dairies. Regulators may also consider safe-harbour provisions that ease penalties for dairy operators who report contamination at their facilities; this could also encourage early disclosure, giving authorities time to save lives.
(Source: Bitter milk: On the Rajamahendravaram milk adulteration case - The Hindu, March 10)
What does the word "lethality" mean in the passage about industrial hazards?
opts: A state of being famous or well-known
expl:
Meaning: lethality = the ability to cause death; deadliness (घातकता, प्राणघातकता).

From lethal = deadly (घातक).

The deciding line.

"an industrial compound already infamous in India for its lethality"

The same passage reports a death toll of 11 — the compound is known for killing.

Answer: The ability to cause death

Why the others are wrong.

• The quality of being very expensive = costliness (महँगापन) — the word for this is expensiveness; cost is never the issue here.

• The process of industrial manufacturing = making goods in factories (औद्योगिक निर्माण) — "industrial" describes the compound, not the meaning of lethality.

• A state of being famous or well-known = fame (प्रसिद्धि) — this is the trap: the fame-word in the line is infamous (कुख्यात — बुरे कारण से प्रसिद्ध), and lethality is the reason for that bad fame.

Infamous = famous for something bad; lethality is what this compound is infamous for.

In the following question, out of the four alternatives, choose the one which gives the correct meaning of the given idiom or phrase.
Mr. Sharma complained that filing tax returns manually every year is a real pain in the neck,
expl:
Meaning: a pain in the neck = a person or thing that is very annoying or troublesome (सिरदर्द, झंझट).

"complained that filing tax returns manually every year" — a repetitive chore he dislikes.

tedious = long, slow and boring (उबाऊ).

Origin.

An early-1900s American phrase, a polite version of ruder "pain in the …" expressions — the nagging ache of a stiff neck stands for something that keeps irritating you.

Answer: (3) The task is tedious and annoying

Why the others are wrong.

• causes physical injury — the literal sense; the idiom names no real pain (शारीरिक चोट).

• very enjoyable — the opposite; for that, a piece of cake or a joy (आनंददायक).

• requires medical expertise — a literal misreading of pain (चिकित्सा विशेषज्ञता).

Complaining is the clue: a pain in the neck is a nuisance, never an injury.

Given below are four jumbled parts of a sentence. Select the option that gives their correct order and forms a meaningful sentence.
P. to automate complex tasks that once
Q. Artificial Intelligence has the potential
R. required human intuition and years of specialized training
S. thereby revolutionizing the modern workforce
expl:
Rule: in a jumbled sentence, find the subject and verb first, then follow each dangling edge — an infinitive after potential, a verb after that, and a thereby participle at the end.

Find the opener.

Q — Artificial Intelligence has the potential — subject + verb, capital letter, no back-reference: it opens.

Follow the edges.

Q → P: the potential to automate — "potential" takes a to-infinitive.

P → R: P ends on that once, which needs a verb; R supplies it — that once required human intuition …

R → S: thereby revolutionizing is a result phrase (जिससे … ) and naturally closes the sentence.

The sentence.

Artificial Intelligence has the potential to automate complex tasks that once required human intuition and years of specialized training, thereby revolutionizing the modern workforce.

Answer: QPRS

Word help.

intuition = understanding something without conscious reasoning (अंतर्ज्ञान).

revolutionizing = changing completely (पूरी तरह बदल देना).

A part ending in "that once" is an open door — the next part must begin with a verb.

qhtml:
Given below are four jumbled parts of a sentence. Select the option that gives their correct order and forms a meaningful sentence.
P. while providing a platform for global connectivity
Q. can also lead to mental health issues
R. excessive use of social media platforms
S. if not balanced with real-world interactions
expl:
⚠️ Note: the official key marks option (c) (RQPS); the better order is option (a) (PRQS), because also in Q needs the benefit in P to come before it, and if not balanced (S) must sit right after the harm in Q that it limits.

Rule: a concessive while-clause (विरोधसूचक उपवाक्य) states the good side first; the main clause then adds the bad side with also; a condition (if not …) attaches to the verb it limits.

Example: While saving time, fast food can also harm health if eaten daily.

Fix the core.

R + Q = subject + verb: excessive use of social media platforms can also lead to mental health issues.

Place S.

if not balanced with real-world interactions limits the harm — mental health issues arise only when use is not balanced.

So S must follow Q directly: Q → S.

Place P.

also in Q means "besides something good already said".

That good thing is P — providing a platform for global connectivity — so P comes first: P → R.

The sentence.

While providing a platform for global connectivity, excessive use of social media platforms can also lead to mental health issues if not balanced with real-world interactions.

Why the key's order is weaker.

RQPS gives … mental health issues while providing a platform for global connectivity if not balanced with real-world interactions.

Here also has no earlier point to add to, and if not balanced now hangs on providing a platform — connectivity does not depend on lack of balance.

Answer: PRQS

Word help.

connectivity = the state of being connected (जुड़ाव, संपर्क).

"Also" looks backward — whatever it adds to must already be in the sentence.

qhtml:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.
The speech of the child impressed the principal and he gave a bouquet to the speaker on the stage.
opts: The principal was impressed by the speech of the child and a bouquet was given to the speaker on the stage by him.
The principal had been impressed by the speech of the child and a bouquet was given to the speaker on the stage by him.
The principal had been impressed by the speech of the child and a bouquet had been given to the speaker on the stage by him.
Being impressed by the speech of the child by the principal, a bouquet was given to the speaker on the stage by him.
expl:
Rule: simple past active → simple past passive (सामान्य भूत कर्मवाच्य): object + was/were + V3 + by + subject.

In a compound sentence joined by and, change each clause separately and keep the tense of each.

Example: She wrote a letter and he posted it. → A letter was written by her and it was posted by him.

Clause 1.

The speech of the child impressed the principal → The principal was impressed by the speech of the child.

Clause 2.

he gave a bouquet to the speaker → a bouquet was given to the speaker on the stage by him.

Answer: (1) The principal was impressed by the speech of the child and a bouquet was given to the speaker on the stage by him.

Why the others are wrong.

• had been impressed — past perfect passive (पूर्ण भूत कर्मवाच्य); the active verb impressed is simple past, so the tense has been changed.

• had been impressed … had been given — both clauses wrongly shifted to past perfect passive.

• Being impressed … by the principal, a bouquet was given — a participle phrase that leaves being impressed dangling on the bouquet (असंबद्ध कृदंत), and "by the principal" is misplaced.

Change the voice, never the tense: impressed → was impressed, gave → was given.

Identify the segment in the sentence, which contains the grammatical error.
Neither Amit nor Raju are staying with his parents in Mumbai.
expl:
Type: Error Detection – "Neither ... nor" Agreement

Rule: With "neither ... nor" joining two singular subjects, the verb is singular, and the pronoun agrees with the nearer subject.

("neither ... nor" के साथ एकवचन क्रिया आती है।)

Corrected sentence

"Neither Amit nor Raju is staying with his parents in Mumbai."

Why the others are correct

qhtml:
Read the passage and answer the questions given below it.
In 18th-century Germany, Baron Munchausen regales his friends, over drinks, with stories of his many adventures. These include his supposed travel to the moon. Long before Neil Armstrong and Edwin Aldrin stepped out of Apollo 11 onto the surface of the moon 50 years ago, on July 20, 1969, the aspiration to travel to this shiny orb in the sky has fired human imagination. A Flight To The Moon by George Fowler, From The Earth To The Moon – and its sequel, Around The Moon – by Jules Verne, The First Men In The Moon by HG Wells, Prelude To Space by Arthur C Clarke… are only a few of the many fictionalised accounts that have, for centuries, reflected this aspiration. In the 1954 Explorers On The Moon, iconic comic book character, Tintin, reaches the moon. While some writers imagined the moon’s surface to be barren and uninhabited, others have written about it being populated with lunar beings. Even when Apollo 11 mission was being planned and worked on, in 1963, Apollo At Go by Jeff Sutton, presented a realistic fictionalised portrayal of the upcoming landing.
The successful landing of Apollo 11 and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin’s walk on the moon, opened up another exciting possibility – could the common man or non-space-scientist reach for the moon? Literally? What had hitherto been in the realm of speculation was now a reality and we weren’t satisfied with just second-hand information any more. Between 1969 and 1972, the US sent six successful manned missions to the moon, and with each victory, the lunar destination seemed a little closer within the reach of the common man.
Who was the first person to speak of travel to the moon?

Text opens: "In 18th-century Germany, Baron Munchausen ... stories of his many adventures ... his supposed travel to the moon." He is the earliest mentioned.

Why the others are wrong

• Armstrong / Sutton / Branson – all came much later.

qhtml:
Read the passage and answer the questions given below it
Our civilization is more secure because it is much more widely spread. Most of the previous civilizations came to an end because uncivilized peoples broke in and destroyed them. This was the fate of Babylon, Assyria, India, China, Greece and Rome. Previous civilizations were specialized and limited like an oasis in a surrounding desert of savagery. Eventually, the desert closed in and the oasis was no more. But to-day, it is the oasis which is spreading over the desert. Practically no part of the world is untouched by it.
For the first time, the world has now a chance of becoming a single whole, a unity. To-day, the food we eat comes from all over the world. The things in a grocer’s shop are from the ends of the earth. There are oranges from Brazil, grapes from Africa, rice from India, tea from china, sugar from Columbia etc.
To-day the world is beginning to look more like one enormous box. Therefore, there is little danger upon our civilization from outside. The danger comes only from within; it is a danger from among us.
To-day, the sharing-out of money – the sharing-out of food, clothing, houses and books, is still very unfair. In England alone, in sharing out of the National Income, we find that one half is divided among every sixteen people and the seventeenth person gets the other half. So while some few people live in luxury, many have not even enough to eat and drink and wear. Again, in England to-day, thousands of people live in dreadful surroundings. There are many families of five or six persons who live in a single room; in this same room they are born and in this same room they die, because, they are too poor to afford another room. Until everyone gets his proper share of necessary and delightful things, our civilization will not be perfect.
What according to the writer was the desert that surrounded the oasis?

Text: "Previous civilizations were ... like an oasis in a surrounding desert of savagery." So the "desert" = savagery.

Why the others are wrong

• Civilization / rich countries / poorer people – the desert stands for savagery (the uncivilized world).

While I waited expectantly, Madame came in and told me that there was no room at all for me in the hotel, not a bed, not a corner. She was extremely friendly and seemed to find a fund of secret amusement in the fact; she looked at me as though expecting me to break into delighted laughter. “To-morrow,” she said, “there may be. I am expecting a young gentleman who is suddenly taken ill to move from number eleven. He is at present at the chemist's perhaps you would care to see the room?”

“But he will be gone,” cried Madame, opening her blue eyes wide and laughing with that French cordiality so enchanting to English hearing. I was too tired and hungry to feel either appreciative or argumentative. “Perhaps you can recommend me another hotel?”

I was the only guest in the dining-room. A tired waiter provided me with an omelet and a pot of coffee, then leaned against a sideboard and watched me while I ate, the limp table napkin over his arm seeming to symbolise the very man.
“Are you ready, Madame?” asked the waiter. “It is I who carry your luggage.”
“Quite ready.”

No one can look back on his schooldays and say with truth that they were altogether unhappy.
I have good memories of St Cyprian's, among a horde of bad ones. Sometimes on summer afternoons there were wonderful expeditions across the Downs to a village called Birling Gap, or to Beachy Head, where one bathed dangerously among the boulders and came home covered with cuts. And there were still more wonderful mid-summer evenings when, as a special treat, we were not driven off to bed as usual but allowed to wander about the grounds in the long twilight, ending up with a plunge into the swimming bathe at about nine o'clock. There was the joy of waking early on summer mornings and getting in an hour's undisturbed reading (Ian Hay, Thackeray, Kipling and H. G. Wells were the favourite authors of my boyhood) in the sunlit, sleeping dormitory. There was also cricket, which I was no good at but with which I conducted a sort of hopeless love affair up to the age of about eighteen. And there was the pleasure of keeping caterpillars — the silky green and purple puss-moth, the ghostly green poplar-hawk, the privet-hawk, large as one's third finger, specimens of which could be illicitly purchased for sixpence at a shop in the town — and, when one could escape long enough from the master who was ‘taking the walk’, there was the excitement of dredging the dew-ponds on the Downs for enormous newts with orange-coloured bellies. This business of being out for a walk, coming across something of fascinating interest and then being dragged away from it by a yell from the master, like a dog jerked onwards by the leash, is an important feature of school life, and helps to build up the conviction, so strong in many children, that the things you most want to do are always unattainable.

Our civilization is more secure because it is much more widely spread. Most of the previous civilizations came to an end because uncivilized peoples broke in and destroyed them. This was the fate of Babylon, Assyria, India, China, Greece and Rome. Previous civilizations were specialized and limited like an oasis in a surrounding desert of savagery. Eventually, the desert closed in and the oasis was no more. But to-day, it is the oasis which is spreading over the desert. Practically no part of the world is untouched by it.
For the first time, the world has now a chance of becoming a single whole, a unity. To-day, the food we eat comes from all over the world. The things in a grocer’s shop are from the ends of the earth. There are oranges from Brazil, grapes from Africa, rice from India, tea from china, sugar from Columbia etc.
To-day the world is beginning to look more like one enormous box. Therefore, there is little danger upon our civilization from outside. The danger comes only from within; it is a danger from among us.
To-day, the sharing-out of money – the sharing-out of food, clothing, houses and books, is still very unfair. In England alone, in sharing out of the National Income, we find that one half is divided among every sixteen people and the seventeenth person gets the other half. So while some few people live in luxury, many have not even enough to eat and drink and wear. Again, in England to-day, thousands of people live in dreadful surroundings. There are many families of five or six persons who live in a single room; in this same room they are born and in this same room they die, because, they are too poor to afford another room. Until everyone gets his proper share of necessary and delightful things, our civilization will not be perfect.

While I waited expectantly, Madame came in and told me that there was no room at all for me in the hotel, not a bed, not a corner. She was extremely friendly and seemed to find a fund of secret amusement in the fact; she looked at me as though expecting me to break into delighted laughter. “To-morrow,” she said, “there may be. I am expecting a young gentleman who is suddenly taken ill to move from number eleven. He is at present at the chemist's perhaps you would care to see the room?”
“Not at all,” said I. “Neither shall I wish tomorrow to sleep in the bedroom of an indisposed young gentleman.”
“But he will be gone,” cried Madame, opening her blue eyes wide and laughing with that French cordiality so enchanting to English hearing. I was too tired and hungry to feel either appreciative or argumentative. “Perhaps you can recommend me another hotel?”
“Impossible!” She shook her head and turned up her eyes, mentally counting over the blue bows painted on the ceiling. “You see, it is the season in Bruges, and people do not care to let their rooms for a very short time” not a glance at my little suit case lying between us, but I looked at it gloomily, and it seemed to dwindle before my desperate gaze become small enough to hold nothing but a collapsible folding tooth-brush.
“My large box is at the station,” I said coldly, buttoning my gloves.
Madame started. “You have more luggage. Then you intend to make a long stay in Bruges, perhaps?”
“At least a fortnight perhaps a month.” I shrugged my shoulders.
“One moment,” said Madame. “I shall see what I can do.” She disappeared, I am sure not further than the other side of the door, for she reappeared immediately and told me I might have a room at her private house “just round the corner and kept by an old servant who, although she has a wall eye, has been in our family for fifteen years. The porter will take you there, and you can have supper before you go.”
I was the only guest in the dining-room. A tired waiter provided me with an omelet and a pot of coffee, then leaned against a sideboard and watched me while I ate, the limp table napkin over his arm seeming to symbolise the very man.
“Are you ready, Madame?” asked the waiter. “It is I who carry your luggage.”
“Quite ready.”

No one can look back on his schooldays and say with truth that they were altogether unhappy.
I have good memories of St Cyprian's, among a horde of bad ones. Sometimes on summer afternoons there were wonderful expeditions across the Downs to a village called Birling Gap, or to Beachy Head, where one bathed dangerously among the boulders and came home covered with cuts. And there were still more wonderful mid-summer evenings when, as a special treat, we were not driven off to bed as usual but allowed to wander about the grounds in the long twilight, ending up with a plunge into the swimming bathe at about nine o'clock. There was the joy of waking early on summer mornings and getting in an hour's undisturbed reading (Ian Hay, Thackeray, Kipling and H. G. Wells were the favourite authors of my boyhood) in the sunlit, sleeping dormitory. There was also cricket, which I was no good at but with which I conducted a sort of hopeless love affair up to the age of about eighteen. And there was the pleasure of keeping caterpillars — the silky green and purple puss-moth, the ghostly green poplar-hawk, the privet-hawk, large as one's third finger, specimens of which could be illicitly purchased for sixpence at a shop in the town — and, when one could escape long enough from the master who was ‘taking the walk’, there was the excitement of dredging the dew-ponds on the Downs for enormous newts with orange-coloured bellies. This business of being out for a walk, coming across something of fascinating interest and then being dragged away from it by a yell from the master, like a dog jerked onwards by the leash, is an important feature of school life, and helps to build up the conviction, so strong in many children, that the things you most want to do are always unattainable.

Read the passage and answer the questions given below it.
In 18th-century Germany, Baron Munchausen regales his friends, over drinks, with stories of his many adventures. These include his supposed travel to the moon. Long before Neil Armstrong and Edwin Aldrin stepped out of Apollo 11 onto the surface of the moon 50 years ago, on July 20, 1969, the aspiration to travel to this shiny orb in the sky has fired human imagination. A Flight To The Moon by George Fowler, From The Earth To The Moon – and its sequel, Around The Moon – by Jules Verne, The First Men In The Moon by HG Wells, Prelude To Space by Arthur C Clarke… are only a few of the many fictionalised accounts that have, for centuries, reflected this aspiration. In the 1954 Explorers On The Moon, iconic comic book character, Tintin, reaches the moon. While some writers imagined the moon’s surface to be barren and uninhabited, others have written about it being populated with lunar beings. Even when Apollo 11 mission was being planned and worked on, in 1963, Apollo At Go by Jeff Sutton, presented a realistic fictionalised portrayal of the upcoming landing.
The successful landing of Apollo 11 and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin’s walk on the moon, opened up another exciting possibility – could the common man or non-space-scientist reach for the moon? Literally? What had hitherto been in the realm of speculation was now a reality and we weren’t satisfied with just second-hand information any more. Between 1969 and 1972, the US sent six successful manned missions to the moon, and with each victory, the lunar destination seemed a little closer within the reach of the common man.
The writer uses the expression ‘literally’ because___
opts: people only dream of doing it
it has been an idiom for desiring something unlikely
no one can ever go to the moon
it is wrong to build up stories
expl:

"could the common man ... reach for the moon? Literally?" — "reach for the moon" is normally an idiom for wanting something unlikely; the writer adds "literally" because now it could actually happen.

Why the others are wrong

• (A) only dream / (C) no one can go / (D) wrong to build stories – miss the idiom-turned-real point.

The children were to be driven, as a special treat, to the sands at Jagborough. Nicholas was not to be of the party; he was in disgrace. Only that morning he had refused to eat his wholesome bread-and-milk on the seemingly frivolous ground that there was a frog in it. Older and wiser and better people(his aunt), had told him that there could not possibly be a frog in his bread-and-milk and that he was not to talk nonsense; he continued, nevertheless, to talk what seemed complete nonsense, and described with much detail the coloration and markings of the alleged frog. qhtml:
Read the passage and answer the questions given below it.
In 18th-century Germany, Baron Munchausen regales his friends, over drinks, with stories of his many adventures. These include his supposed travel to the moon. Long before Neil Armstrong and Edwin Aldrin stepped out of Apollo 11 onto the surface of the moon 50 years ago, on July 20, 1969, the aspiration to travel to this shiny orb in the sky has fired human imagination. A Flight To The Moon by George Fowler, From The Earth To The Moon – and its sequel, Around The Moon – by Jules Verne, The First Men In The Moon by HG Wells, Prelude To Space by Arthur C Clarke… are only a few of the many fictionalised accounts that have, for centuries, reflected this aspiration. In the 1954 Explorers On The Moon, iconic comic book character, Tintin, reaches the moon. While some writers imagined the moon’s surface to be barren and uninhabited, others have written about it being populated with lunar beings. Even when Apollo 11 mission was being planned and worked on, in 1963, Apollo At Go by Jeff Sutton, presented a realistic fictionalised portrayal of the upcoming landing.
The successful landing of Apollo 11 and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin’s walk on the moon, opened up another exciting possibility – could the common man or non-space-scientist reach for the moon? Literally? What had hitherto been in the realm of speculation was now a reality and we weren’t satisfied with just second-hand information any more. Between 1969 and 1972, the US sent six successful manned missions to the moon, and with each victory, the lunar destination seemed a little closer within the reach of the common man.
Which of the following statements is not true according to the passage?
opts: Someday the common man could make a trip to the moon.
Man’s walk on the moon inspired scientists to plan more expeditions.
All the writers wrote about the moon being inhabited by weird creatures.
Man has always been attracted to the moon.
expl:
How to locate the answer (NOT-true question)

Text: "some writers imagined the moon's surface to be barren and uninhabited, others wrote about it being populated with lunar beings." So NOT all wrote about creatures → (C) is false.

Why the others are true

• (A) common man could go, (B) the walk inspired more expeditions, (D) man always attracted to the moon – all supported.
raw_sol:
✅ Correct Answer: Option C (All the writers wrote about the moon being inhabited by weird creatures)

How to locate the answer (NOT-true question)

Text: "some writers imagined the moon's surface to be barren and uninhabited, others wrote about it being populated with lunar beings." So NOT all wrote about creatures → (C) is false.

Why the others are true

•(A) common man could go, (B) the walk inspired more expeditions, (D) man always attracted to the moon – all supported.

No one can look back on his schooldays and say with truth that they were altogether unhappy.
I have good memories of St Cyprian's, among a horde of bad ones. Sometimes on summer afternoons there were wonderful expeditions across the Downs to a village called Birling Gap, or to Beachy Head, where one bathed dangerously among the boulders and came home covered with cuts. And there were still more wonderful mid-summer evenings when, as a special treat, we were not driven off to bed as usual but allowed to wander about the grounds in the long twilight, ending up with a plunge into the swimming bathe at about nine o'clock. There was the joy of waking early on summer mornings and getting in an hour's undisturbed reading (Ian Hay, Thackeray, Kipling and H. G. Wells were the favourite authors of my boyhood) in the sunlit, sleeping dormitory. There was also cricket, which I was no good at but with which I conducted a sort of hopeless love affair up to the age of about eighteen. And there was the pleasure of keeping caterpillars — the silky green and purple puss-moth, the ghostly green poplar-hawk, the privet-hawk, large as one's third finger, specimens of which could be illicitly purchased for sixpence at a shop in the town — and, when one could escape long enough from the master who was ‘taking the walk’, there was the excitement of dredging the dew-ponds on the Downs for enormous newts with orange-coloured bellies. This business of being out for a walk, coming across something of fascinating interest and then being dragged away from it by a yell from the master, like a dog jerked onwards by the leash, is an important feature of school life, and helps to build up the conviction, so strong in many children, that the things you most want to do are always unattainable.

While I waited expectantly, Madame came in and told me that there was no room at all for me in the hotel, not a bed, not a corner. She was extremely friendly and seemed to find a fund of secret amusement in the fact; she looked at me as though expecting me to break into delighted laughter. “To-morrow,” she said, “there may be. I am expecting a young gentleman who is suddenly taken ill to move from number eleven. He is at present at the chemist's perhaps you would care to see the room?”
“Not at all,” said I. “Neither shall I wish tomorrow to sleep in the bedroom of an indisposed young gentleman.”
“But he will be gone,” cried Madame, opening her blue eyes wide and laughing with that French cordiality so enchanting to English hearing. I was too tired and hungry to feel either appreciative or argumentative. “Perhaps you can recommend me another hotel?”
“Impossible!” She shook her head and turned up her eyes, mentally counting over the blue bows painted on the ceiling. “You see, it is the season in Bruges, and people do not care to let their rooms for a very short time” not a glance at my little suit case lying between us, but I looked at it gloomily, and it seemed to dwindle before my desperate gaze become small enough to hold nothing but a collapsible folding tooth-brush.
“My large box is at the station,” I said coldly, buttoning my gloves.
Madame started. “You have more luggage. Then you intend to make a long stay in Bruges, perhaps?”
“At least a fortnight perhaps a month.” I shrugged my shoulders.
“One moment,” said Madame. “I shall see what I can do.” She disappeared, I am sure not further than the other side of the door, for she reappeared immediately and told me I might have a room at her private house “just round the corner and kept by an old servant who, although she has a wall eye, has been in our family for fifteen years. The porter will take you there, and you can have supper before you go.”
I was the only guest in the dining-room. A tired waiter provided me with an omelet and a pot of coffee, then leaned against a sideboard and watched me while I ate, the limp table napkin over his arm seeming to symbolise the very man.
“Are you ready, Madame?” asked the waiter. “It is I who carry your luggage.”
“Quite ready.”

The children were to be driven, as a special treat, to the sands at Jagborough. Nicholas was not to be of the party; he was in disgrace. Only that morning he had refused to eat his wholesome bread-and-milk on the seemingly frivolous ground that there was a frog in it. Older and wiser and better people(his aunt), had told him that there could not possibly be a frog in his bread-and-milk and that he was not to talk nonsense; he continued, nevertheless, to talk what seemed complete nonsense, and described with much detail the coloration and markings of the alleged frog. The dramatic part of the incident was that there really was a frog in Nicholas's basin of bread-and-milk; he had put it there himself, so he felt entitled to know something about it. The sin of taking a frog from the garden and putting it into a bowl of wholesome bread-and-milk was enlarged on at great length, but the fact that stood out clearest in the whole affair, as it presented itself to the mind of Nicholas, was that the older, wiser, and better people had been proved to be profoundly in error in matters about which they had expressed the utmost assurance.

Our civilization is more secure because it is much more widely spread. Most of the previous civilizations came to an end because uncivilized peoples broke in and destroyed them. This was the fate of Babylon, Assyria, India, China, Greece and Rome. Previous civilizations were specialized and limited like an oasis in a surrounding desert of savagery. Eventually, the desert closed in and the oasis was no more. But to-day, it is the oasis which is spreading over the desert. Practically no part of the world is untouched by it.
For the first time, the world has now a chance of becoming a single whole, a unity. To-day, the food we eat comes from all over the world. The things in a grocer’s shop are from the ends of the earth. There are oranges from Brazil, grapes from Africa, rice from India, tea from china, sugar from Columbia etc.
To-day the world is beginning to look more like one enormous box. Therefore, there is little danger upon our civilization from outside. The danger comes only from within; it is a danger from among us.

No one can look back on his schooldays and say with truth that they were altogether unhappy.
I have good memories of St Cyprian's, among a horde of bad ones. Sometimes on summer afternoons there were wonderful expeditions across the Downs to a village called Birling Gap, or to Beachy Head, where one bathed dangerously among the boulders and came home covered with cuts. And there were still more wonderful mid-summer evenings when, as a special treat, we were not driven off to bed as usual but allowed to wander about the grounds in the long twilight, ending up with a plunge into the swimming bathe at about nine o'clock. There was the joy of waking early on summer mornings and getting in an hour's undisturbed reading (Ian Hay, Thackeray, Kipling and H. G. Wells were the favourite authors of my boyhood) in the sunlit, sleeping dormitory. There was also cricket, which I was no good at but with which I conducted a sort of hopeless love affair up to the age of about eighteen. And there was the pleasure of keeping caterpillars — the silky green and purple puss-moth, the ghostly green poplar-hawk, the privet-hawk, large as one's third finger, specimens of which could be illicitly purchased for sixpence at a shop in the town — and, when one could escape long enough from the master who was ‘taking the walk’, there was the excitement of dredging the dew-ponds on the Downs for enormous newts with orange-coloured bellies. This business of being out for a walk, coming across something of fascinating interest and then being dragged away from it by a yell from the master, like a dog jerked onwards by the leash, is an important feature of school life, and helps to build up the conviction, so strong in many children, that the things you most want to do are always unattainable.

No one can look back on his schooldays and say with truth that they were altogether unhappy.
I have good memories of St Cyprian's, among a horde of bad ones. Sometimes on summer afternoons there were wonderful expeditions across the Downs to a village called Birling Gap, or to Beachy Head, where one bathed dangerously among the boulders and came home covered with cuts. And there were still more wonderful mid-summer evenings when, as a special treat, we were not driven off to bed as usual but allowed to wander about the grounds in the long twilight, ending up with a plunge into the swimming bathe at about nine o'clock. There was the joy of waking early on summer mornings and getting in an hour's undisturbed reading (Ian Hay, Thackeray, Kipling and H. G. Wells were the favourite authors of my boyhood) in the sunlit, sleeping dormitory. There was also cricket, which I was no good at but with which I conducted a sort of hopeless love affair up to the age of about eighteen. And there was the pleasure of keeping caterpillars — the silky green and purple puss-moth, the ghostly green poplar-hawk, the privet-hawk, large as one's third finger, specimens of which could be illicitly purchased for sixpence at a shop in the town — and, when one could escape long enough from the master who was ‘taking the walk’, there was the excitement of dredging the dew-ponds on the Downs for enormous newts with orange-coloured bellies. This business of being out for a walk, coming across something of fascinating interest and then being dragged away from it by a yell from the master, like a dog jerked onwards by the leash, is an important feature of school life, and helps to build up the conviction, so strong in many children, that the things you most want to do are always unattainable.

qhtml:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
The term ‘dietary fibres’ refers collectively to indigestible carbohydrates present in plant foods. The importance of these dietary fibres came into the picture when it was observed that the people taking a diet rich in these fibres had low incidence of coronary heart disease, irritable bowel syndrome, dental caries and gall stones.
The foodstuffs rich in these dietary fibres are cereals and grains, legumes, fruits with seeds, citrus fruits, carrots, cabbage, green leafy vegetables, apples, melons, peaches, pears etc. These dietary fibres are not digested by the enzymes of the stomach and the small intestine. They have the property of holding water and because of it, these get swollen and behave like a sponge as these pass through the gastrointestinal tract. The fibres add bulk to the diet and increase transit time in the gut and decrease the time of release of ingested food in the colon. These fibres hold water so the stools are soft, bulky and readily eliminated.
In recent years, it has been considered essential to have some amount of fibres in the diet. Their beneficial effects lie in preventing heart disease and decreasing cholesterol level. The fibres like gum and pectin are reported to decrease post prandial (after meals) glucose level in blood. They are also recommended for the management of certain types of diabetes.
The fibres increase motility of the small intestine and the colon and so there is less time for exposure of the mucosa to harmful toxic substances. Therefore, there is a less desire to eat and the energy intake can be maintained within the range of requirement. This phenomenon helps in keeping a check on obesity.
The dietary fibres may have some adverse effects on nutrition by binding some trace metals like calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, zinc and others and therefore preventing their proper absorption. This may pose a possibility of nutritional deficiency especially when diets contain marginal levels of mineral elements. This may put constraints on increasing dietary fibres. It is suggested that an intake of 40 gram dietary fibres per day is desirable.
What is the theme of the passage?
expl:
How to locate the answer

The passage repeatedly stresses the benefits/importance of fibres — preventing heart disease, lowering cholesterol, controlling glucose and obesity. So the theme is the importance of dietary fibres.

Why the others are wrong

• Sources / functioning of intestines / balanced diet – these are details inside the passage, not the overall theme.

✅ Correct Answer: Option B (Importance of dietary fibres)

My grandmother and I were good friends. My parents left me with her when they went to live in the city and we were constantly together. She used to wake me up in the morning and get me ready for school. She said her morning prayer in a monotonous sing-song while she bathed and dressed me in the hope that I would listen and get to know it by heart; I listened because I loved her voice but never bothered to learn it. Then she would fetch my wooden slate which she had already washed and plastered with yellow chalk, a tiny earthen ink-pot and a red pen, tie them all in a bundle and hand it to me. After a breakfast of a thick, stale chapatti with a little butter and sugar spread on it, we went to school. She carried several stale chapattis with her for the village dogs.
My grandmother always went to school with me because the school was attached to the temple. The priest taught us the alphabet and the morning prayer. While the children sat in rows on either side of the verandah singing the alphabet or the prayer in a chorus, my grandmother sat inside reading the scriptures. When we had both finished, we would walk back together. This time the village dogs would meet us at the temple door. They followed us to our home growling and fighting with each other for the chapattis we threw to them. When my parents were comfortably settled in the city, they sent for us. That was a turning-point in our friendship. Although we shared the same room, my grandmother no longer came to school with me. I used to go to an English school in a motor bus. There were no dogs in the streets and she took to feeding sparrows in the courtyard of our city house. As the years rolled by we saw less of each other. For some time she continued to wake me up and get me ready for school. When I came back she would ask me what the teacher had taught me. I would tell her English words and little things of western science and learning, the law of gravity, Archimedes’ Principle, the world being round, etc. This made her unhappy. She could not help me with my lessons. She did not believe in the things they taught at the English school and was distressed that there was no teaching about God and the scriptures.
Why did the grandmother accompany her grandson to school every day?

To ensure he wouldn’t run away to play in the streets
To read scriptures in the temple while he studied
To keep him safe from stray dogs
expl:

• (A) spend time / (B) stop him playing / (D) protect from dogs – not the reason given.

✅ Correct Answer: Option C (To read scriptures in the temple while he studied)

Text: "the school was attached to the temple ... my grandmother sat inside reading the scriptures" while the children studied.

Why the others are wrong

•(A) spend time / (B) stop him playing / (D) protect from dogs – not the reason given.

Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
The term ‘dietary fibres’ refers collectively to indigestible carbohydrates present in plant foods. The importance of these dietary fibres came into the picture when it was observed that the people taking a diet rich in these fibres had low incidence of coronary heart disease, irritable bowel syndrome, dental caries and gall stones.
The foodstuffs rich in these dietary fibres are cereals and grains, legumes, fruits with seeds, citrus fruits, carrots, cabbage, green leafy vegetables, apples, melons, peaches, pears etc. These dietary fibres are not digested by the enzymes of the stomach and the small intestine. They have the property of holding water and because of it, these get swollen and behave like a sponge as these pass through the gastrointestinal tract. The fibres add bulk to the diet and increase transit time in the gut and decrease the time of release of ingested food in the colon. These fibres hold water so the stools are soft, bulky and readily eliminated.
In recent years, it has been considered essential to have some amount of fibres in the diet. Their beneficial effects lie in preventing heart disease and decreasing cholesterol level. The fibres like gum and pectin are reported to decrease post prandial (after meals) glucose level in blood. They are also recommended for the management of certain types of diabetes.
The fibres increase motility of the small intestine and the colon and so there is less time for exposure of the mucosa to harmful toxic substances. Therefore, there is a less desire to eat and the energy intake can be maintained within the range of requirement. This phenomenon helps in keeping a check on obesity.
The dietary fibres may have some adverse effects on nutrition by binding some trace metals like calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, zinc and others and therefore preventing their proper absorption. This may pose a possibility of nutritional deficiency especially when diets contain marginal levels of mineral elements. This may put constraints on increasing dietary fibres. It is suggested that an intake of 40 gram dietary fibres per day is desirable.
What are dietary fibres?
expl:
How to locate the answer

Opening line: "'dietary fibres' refers collectively to indigestible carbohydrates present in plant foods." That is the definition.

Why the others are wrong

• Enzymes / ingested food in the colon / easily digestible food – the text clearly says fibres are indigestible, so these are wrong.

✅ Correct Answer: Option C (Indigestible carbohydrates in plant foods)

•Enzymes / ingested food in the colon / easily digestible food – the text clearly says fibres are indigestible, so these are wrong.

Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
The methods of embalming, or treating the dead body, that the ancient Egyptians used is called ‘mummification’. Using special processes, the Egyptians removed all moisture from the body, leaving only a dried form that would not easily decay. It was important in their religion to preserve the dead body in as life-like a manner as possible.
The mummification process took seventy days. Special priests worked as embalmers, treating and wrapping the body. Beyond knowing the correct rituals and prayers to be performed at various stages, the priests also needed a detailed knowledge of human anatomy. The first step in the process was the removal of all internal parts that might decay rapidly. The brain was removed by carefully inserting special hooked instruments up through the nostrils in order to pull out bits of brain tissue. The embalmers then removed the organs of the abdomen and chest through a cut usually made on the left side of the abdomen. They left only the heart in place, believing it to be the center of a person's being and intelligence. The other organs were preserved separately, with the stomach, liver, lungs and intestines placed in special boxes or jars, today called ‘canopic jars’. These were buried with the mummy.
The embalmers next removed all moisture from the body. This they did by covering the body with ‘natron’, a type of salt which has great drying properties, and by placing additional natron packets inside the body. When the body had dried out completely, embalmers removed the internal packets and lightly washed the natron off the body. The result was a very dried-out but recognizable human form. To make the mummy seem even more life-like, sunken areas of the body were filled out with linen and other materials and false eyes were added.
Next the wrapping began. Each mummy needed hundreds of yards of linen. The priests carefully wound the long strips of linen around the body, sometimes even wrapping each finger and toe separately before wrapping the entire hand or foot. In order to protect the dead from mishap in after life, amulets were placed among the wrappings and prayers and magical words written on some of the linen strips. Often the priests placed a mask of the person's face between the layers of head bandages. At last, the priests wrapped the final cloth or shroud in place and secured it with linen strips. The mummy was complete. It was then placed in the tomb along with food, furniture, vessels, perfumes, jewels and other things required in the afterlife.
Which of the following was NOT buried with the mummies?
expl:
How to locate the answer (NOT-buried question)

Buried with the mummy were canopic jars, amulets, perfumes (and food, jewels...). The embalmers were the priests who did the work — they were not buried. So (A) is the answer.

✅ Correct Answer: Option A (Embalmers)

How to locate the answer (NOT-buried question)

The methods of embalming, or treating the dead body, that the ancient Egyptians used is called ‘mummification’. Using special processes, the Egyptians removed all moisture from the body, leaving only a dried form that would not easily decay. It was important in their religion to preserve the dead body in as life-like a manner as possible.
The mummification process took seventy days. Special priests worked as embalmers, treating and wrapping the body. Beyond knowing the correct rituals and prayers to be performed at various stages, the priests also needed a detailed knowledge of human anatomy. The first step in the process was the removal of all internal parts that might decay rapidly. The brain was removed by carefully inserting special hooked instruments up through the nostrils in order to pull out bits of brain tissue. The embalmers then removed the organs of the abdomen and chest through a cut usually made on the left side of the abdomen. They left only the heart in place, believing it to be the center of a person's being and intelligence. The other organs were preserved separately, with the stomach, liver, lungs and intestines placed in special boxes or jars, today called ‘canopic jars’. These were buried with the mummy.
The embalmers next removed all moisture from the body. This they did by covering the body with ‘natron’, a type of salt which has great drying properties, and by placing additional natron packets inside the body. When the body had dried out completely, embalmers removed the internal packets and lightly washed the natron off the body. The result was a very dried-out but recognizable human form. To make the mummy seem even more life-like, sunken areas of the body were filled out with linen and other materials and false eyes were added.
Next the wrapping began. Each mummy needed hundreds of yards of linen. The priests carefully wound the long strips of linen around the body, sometimes even wrapping each finger and toe separately before wrapping the entire hand or foot. In order to protect the dead from mishap in after life, amulets were placed among the wrappings and prayers and magical words written on some of the linen strips. Often the priests placed a mask of the person's face between the layers of head bandages. At last, the priests wrapped the final cloth or shroud in place and secured it with linen strips. The mummy was complete. It was then placed in the tomb along with food, furniture, vessels, perfumes, jewels and other things required in the afterlife.
stem: Which of the following was NOT buried with the mummies?

Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.
He told you that he had not known that it was your birthday that day.
opts: You said to him, “I do not know that it is your birthday today.”

• (A) "You said to him" – wrong speaker.

• (D) "I do not know ... that day" – wrong tense/word.

Given below are six sentences A-F, of which A and F are static and B-E have been jumbled. Pick the option that gives the correct order of the jumbled sentences.
A. One day I went to school with four rupees in my pocket to pay the school fees.
B. All through the day, the coins sat quietly in my pocket.
C. So, I was told that the fees would be collected the next day.
D. When school got over, the coins in my pocket began to speak.
E. But the teacher who was to collect the fees was absent.
F. They said that money was meant to be spent on good things like hot ‘jalebis’.
expl:
Type: Para Jumble (A & F fixed)

• A – one day I went to school with four rupees to pay the fees.

• E – but the teacher who was to collect the fees was absent.

• C – so I was told the fees would be collected the next day.

• B – all through the day the coins sat quietly in my pocket.

• D – when school got over, the coins began to speak.

• F – they said money was meant to be spent on hot 'jalebis'.

Order → A-E-C-B-D-F.
raw_sol:
✅ Correct Answer: Option B (AECBDF)

•E – but the teacher who was to collect the fees was absent.

•C – so I was told the fees would be collected the next day.

•B – all through the day the coins sat quietly in my pocket.

•D – when school got over, the coins began to speak.

qhtml:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
When Tao Ying rides on the bus alone, quite often she does not bother to buy a ticket. Why should she? Without her, the bus would still be stopping at every stop, a driver and a conductor would still have to be employed, and the same amount of petrol used. Clearly Tao Ying has to be astute. When the bus conductor looked like the responsible type, she would buy a ticket as soon as she got on board. But if he appeared to be casual and careless, she would not dream of paying, considering it a small punishment for him and a little saving for herself.
Today she is with her son Xiao Ye. She follows him onto the bus. As the doors shut her jacket is caught, ballooning up like a tent behind her. She twists this way and that, finally wrenching herself free. ‘Mama, tickets!’ Xiao Ye says. Children are often more conscious of rituals than adults. Without a ticket in his hand, the ride doesn’t count as a proper ride. On the peeling paint of the door somebody has painted the shape of a pale finger. It points at a number: 1.10 m. Between Xiao Ye ’s round head and the tip of the painted digit setting out the height requirement for a ticket rests the beautiful slender fingers of Tao Ying. ‘Xiao Ye, you are not quite tall enough, still one centimetre away,’ she tells him softly.
‘Mama! I’m tall enough, I’m tall enough!’ Xiao Ye shouts at the top of his voice, stamping on the floor as if it were a tin drum. ‘You told me the last time I could have a ticket the next time, this is the next time. You don’t keep your word!’ He looks up at his mother angrily. Tao Ying looks down at her son. A ticket costs twenty cents. Twenty cents is not to be scoffed at. It can buy a cucumber, two tomatoes or, at a reduced price, three bunches of radishes or enough spinach to last four days. But Xiao Ye’s face is raised up like a half-open blossom, waiting to receive his promise from the sun. She says, ‘Two tickets, please.’ The fierce conductor has beady eyes. ‘This child is one centimetre short of requiring a ticket.’
Xiao Ye shrinks, not just one but several centimetres— the need for a ticket has all of a sudden become interwoven with the pride of a small child. To be able to purchase self-esteem with twenty cents is something that can only happen in childhood and certainly no mother can resist an opportunity to make her son happy. ‘I would like to buy two tickets,’ she says politely.
Xiao Ye was eager to buy a bus ticket because he:
opts: wanted to feel like a grown up
expl:
How to locate the answer

A ticket makes "the ride ... count as a proper ride"; it is tied to "the pride of a small child" — the boy wants to feel grown up.

Why the others are wrong

• (A) responsible, (B) saved money, (C) grown taller – he was actually 1 cm short, so (C) is false; the real reason is childish pride.

Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
Vasco Da Gama was the first European to find an ocean trading route to India. He accomplished what many explorers before him could not do. His discovery of this sea route helped the Portuguese establish a long-lasting colonial empire in Asia and Africa. The new ocean route around Africa allowed Portuguese sailors to avoid the Arab trading hold in the Mediterranean and Middle East. Vasco da Gama opened a new world of riches by opening up an Indian Ocean route. His voyage and explorations helped change the world for Europeans.
Vasco da Gama’s maritime career was during the period when Portugal was searching for a trade route around Africa to India. The Ottoman Empire controlled almost all European trade routes to Asia. This meant they could, and did, charge high prices for ships passing through ports. When Manuel I became King of Portugal in 1495, he continued efforts to open a trade route to India by going around Africa. Although other people were considered for the job, Manuel I finally chose 37-year-old Vasco da Gama for this task.
On 8 July 1497, Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon with a fleet of four ships and a crew of 170 men. Da Gama commanded the Sao Gabriel. Paulo da Gama – brother to Vasco – commanded the São Rafael, a three mast ship. They sailed past the Canary Islands, and reached the Cape Verde islands and then continued sailing, though storms still delayed them for a while. They rounded the cape of Good Hope on 22 November and anchored at Mossel Bay, South Africa. They began sailing again and continued until they reached the Rio dos Bons Sinais (River of Good Omens). Here they erected a statue in the name of Portugal.
They stayed here for a month because much of the crew were sick from scurvy – a disease caused by lack of Vitamin C. Da Gama’s fleet eventually began sailing again. Finally, on 20 May 1498 they reached India. They headed for Kappad, near the large city of Calicut. In Calicut, da Gama met with the king. But the king of Calicut was not impressed with da Gama, and the gifts he brought as offering. They spent several months trading in India, and studying their customs. They left India at the end of August.
Which of the following statements is NOT true?

When Manuel I became King of Portugal in 1495, he continued efforts to open a trade route to India by going around Africa. Although other people were considered for the job, Manuel I finally chose 37-year-old Vasco da Gama for this task.
On 8 July 1497, Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon with a fleet of four ships and a crew of 170 men. Da Gama commanded the Sao Gabriel. Paulo da Gama – brother to Vasco – commanded the São Rafael, a three mast ship. They sailed past the Canary Islands, and reached the Cape Verde islands and then continued sailing, though storms still delayed them for a while. They rounded the cape of Good Hope on 22 November and anchored at Mossel Bay, South Africa. They began sailing again and continued until they reached the Rio dos Bons Sinais (River of Good Omens). Here they erected a statue in the name of Portugal.
They stayed here for a month because much of the crew were sick from scurvy – a disease caused by lack of Vitamin C. Da Gama’s fleet eventually began sailing again. Finally, on 20 May 1498 they reached India. They headed for Kappad, near the large city of Calicut. In Calicut, da Gama met with the king. But the king of Calicut was not impressed with da Gama, and the gifts he brought as offering. They spent several months trading in India, and studying their customs. They left India at the end of August.
